units.translation: armor. The scholiast and other grammarians explain it as πανοπλία [full armor]: Hesychius, "the whole panoply, or a covering wrap." See Thes. vol. 7 p. 12.

The grammarians disagreed about the accent. Arcadius p. 104, 25: "τὸ μέντοι σαγή τὸ πλῆθος τινὲς μὲν ὀξύνουσι, τινὲς δὲ βαρύνουσιν [the word σαγή in the plural some accent on the last syllable, others on the first]." In Eur. Rhes. 207 the Vatican codex has σάγη [armor] in the text, but in the scholium ἡ σαγή [the armor] (codex σφαγή [slaughter]) with acute accent, according to Herodian. In M Sept. 391 σαγαῖς [with armors] and Pers. 240 σαγαί [armors], but σάγην [armor] Ch. 560 and σάγῃ [with armor] 675.

where in M δορυσσόοις (δορύσόοις in the apograph) σαγαῖς [with spear-shaking armors] the letters σ σαγαῖς are written over an erasure of five letters: from which I restored δορυσόῳ σαγᾷ [with spear-shaking armor].
the word σαγή in the plural some accent on the last syllable, others on the first
slaughter) with acute accent, according to Herodian
the whole panoply, or a covering wrap
to fawn, to wag the tail
by fawning to turn aside, as Blomfield explains.
It is constructed with the dative in the sense of serving.
The passive σαίνομαι [I am fawned upon] means to be soothed.
On the use of this verb, which is properly said of dogs that fawn with their tails, Blomfield has written copiously in his glossary on Persians 379 and in Thes. vol. 7 p. 21.

The example is uncertain. where the meter requires ποτισαίνουσα [fawning upon], which is Hermann's conjecture, more probable than Seidler's, who, deleting the words τὸ πρῶτον παράγει [first leads astray], conjectured φιλόφρων γὰρ παρασαίνει βροτὸν εἰς ἄρκυας ῎Ατα [for friendly Ate fawns upon mortals into her nets]: about which I have spoken under προσσαίνω [to fawn upon]. But for ἄρκυας Ἄτα [the nets of Ate] in M is written ἀρκύστατα [net-like], which Hermann corrected by comparing the scholiast's note on ῎Ατη [Ate], rightly, except that he should have written ἄρκυας Ἄτας [the nets of Ate], as Hartung later did: for the subject of the verb παράγει [leads astray] is not "Ατα [Ate], but δολόμητις ἀπάτα θεοῦ [the wily deceit of a god], which the scholiast understood, who on φιλόφρων [friendly] noted ἡ θεῶν ἀπάτη [the deceit of the gods] and undoubtedly read the genitive ῎Ατας [of Ate].
What mortal man can escape the wily deceit of a god? For friendly at first, Ate leads him astray into her nets.
to fawn with watery friendship upon things that seem from a kindly mind.
to fawn upon death and battle with cowardice.
Why then should we still fawn upon destructive death?
bright-eyed, fawning upon the hand and by the belly's needs.
for friendly Ate fawns upon mortals into her nets
the wily deceit of a god
slaughtering a bull over a black-bound shield.
a clangor at the gates of bronze-bound shields.
in the middle of the shield.
having the unburied body of the earth-born one on the shield.
